title: An Explanation for the Absence of Extraterrestrials on Earth
source: Hart 1975; Quarterly Journal of the Royal Astronomical Society 16:128-135

claims.title: Absence premise
claims.detail: Hart framed the problem around the apparent absence of extraterrestrial visitors or artifacts on Earth.

claims.title: Travel-time argument
claims.detail: Hart argued that interstellar travel times are short compared with the age of the Galaxy under some assumptions about technological civilizations.

claims.title: Colonization inference
claims.detail: Hart argued that if extraterrestrial civilizations capable of interstellar expansion had arisen sufficiently long ago and expanded, evidence of their presence should be observable.

claims.title: Rejected explanations
claims.detail: Hart discussed several proposed explanations for the absence of extraterrestrials, including physical difficulty, lack of interest, and deliberate avoidance.

claims.title: Conclusion about technological civilizations
claims.detail: Hart concluded that the absence of observed extraterrestrial presence was evidence against the existence of other advanced civilizations in the Galaxy under his expansion assumptions.

title: Extraterrestrial Intelligent Beings Do Not Exist
source: Tipler 1980; Quarterly Journal of the Royal Astronomical Society 21:267-281

claims.title: Self-replicating probe premise
claims.detail: Tipler considered self-replicating interstellar probes as a mechanism by which a technological civilization could explore or colonize the Galaxy.

claims.title: Replication amplification
claims.detail: The argument relies on the idea that probes able to reproduce using extraterrestrial resources could expand the search or colonization front without requiring a civilization to send probes individually to every star.

claims.title: Galaxy exploration inference
claims.detail: Tipler argued that if such probe-using civilizations existed and chose expansion, their probes should already have reached the Solar System.

claims.title: Non-observation premise
claims.detail: The paper treated the absence of observed probes or extraterrestrial artifacts as an important datum.

claims.title: Strong conclusion
claims.detail: Tipler drew a strong conclusion that extraterrestrial intelligent beings do not exist, conditional on the assumptions about probe feasibility and expansion behavior.

title: The Solipsist Approach to Extraterrestrial Intelligence
source: Sagan and Newman 1983; Quarterly Journal of the Royal Astronomical Society 24:113-121

claims.title: Colonization-wave critique
claims.detail: Sagan and Newman criticized simple arguments that assume stable and inevitable exponential colonization across the Galaxy.

claims.title: Social and ecological constraints
claims.detail: The paper discussed the possibility that civilizations may not sustain unlimited expansion because of social, ecological, or stability constraints.

claims.title: Behavioral assumption
claims.detail: The argument emphasized that conclusions from non-observation depend on assumptions about the motivations and behaviors of extraterrestrial civilizations.

claims.title: Non-observation interpretation
claims.detail: The paper did not treat the absence of visitors as a simple proof that extraterrestrial intelligence is absent.

claims.title: Zoo hypothesis formulation
claims.detail: Ball proposed that advanced extraterrestrial civilizations might deliberately avoid open contact with Earth.

claims.title: Non-contact explanation
claims.detail: The hypothesis interprets absence of contact as compatible with the existence of extraterrestrial civilizations if they follow a non-interference policy.

claims.title: Behavioral dependence
claims.detail: The explanation depends on assumptions about coordinated behavior, restraint, or policy among advanced civilizations.

claims.title: Observability implication
claims.detail: Under the zoo hypothesis, non-detection is not direct evidence that civilizations are absent.

title: Five- or Six-Step Scenario for Evolution?
source: Carter 2008; International Journal of Astrobiology 7(3-4):177-182; DOI 10.1017/S1473550408004023

claims.title: Hard-step framework
claims.detail: Carter discussed an evolutionary hard-step framework in which several difficult transitions may be required before intelligent observers arise.

claims.title: Timescale comparison
claims.detail: The hard-step argument compares the time required for intelligence to emerge with the finite habitable lifetime of a planet.

claims.title: Multiple-step scenario
claims.detail: The paper considered scenarios involving approximately five or six major evolutionary steps.

claims.title: Rarity implication
claims.detail: If multiple evolutionary transitions are hard, then intelligent observers may be rare even if habitable planets are common.

title: Implications of an Anthropic Model of Evolution for Emergence of Complex Life and Intelligence

claims.title: Anthropic evolutionary model
claims.detail: Watson modeled the emergence of complex life and intelligence using an anthropic hard-step framework.

claims.title: Finite habitability window
claims.detail: The model treats Earth's future habitability window as finite and uses this timescale in estimating the number and difficulty of evolutionary steps.

claims.title: Number of steps estimate
claims.detail: Watson argued that the timing of key evolutionary events is consistent with a small number of difficult evolutionary steps.

claims.title: Probability implication
claims.detail: The model implies that complex life and intelligence may be uncommon if several difficult steps are required within a planet's habitable window.

title: Prevalence of Earth-size Planets Orbiting Sun-like Stars
source: Petigura, Howard, and Marcy 2013; PNAS 110(48):19273-19278; DOI 10.1073/pnas.1319909110

claims.title: Kepler occurrence study
claims.detail: The study used Kepler data to estimate occurrence rates of Earth-size planets around Sun-like stars.

claims.title: Earth-size planet frequency
claims.detail: The authors estimated that a substantial fraction of Sun-like stars have Earth-size planets receiving Earth-like stellar flux.

claims.title: Habitable-zone planet implication
claims.detail: The result implies that potentially temperate, Earth-size planets are not extremely rare around Sun-like stars.

claims.title: Planet occurrence scope
claims.detail: The study estimates planet occurrence, not the occurrence of life, intelligence, technology, or detectable civilizations.

title: A New Empirical Constraint on the Prevalence of Technological Species in the Universe

claims.title: Exoplanet-informed Drake framing
claims.detail: Frank and Sullivan used exoplanet occurrence constraints to reformulate part of the Drake equation around the probability of technological species per habitable-zone planet.

claims.title: Humanity-not-first threshold
claims.detail: The paper reported a very low probability threshold above which humanity is unlikely to be the first technological species ever to arise in the observable universe.

claims.title: Milky Way versus universe distinction
claims.detail: The analysis distinguishes between the probability of prior technological species in the observable universe and the probability of currently coexisting civilizations in the Milky Way.

claims.title: Lifetime limitation
claims.detail: The paper does not by itself establish how long technological civilizations remain detectable or whether they expand.

title: How Much SETI Has Been Done? Finding Needles in the n-Dimensional Cosmic Haystack
source: Wright, Kanodia, and Lubar 2018; The Astronomical Journal 156:260; DOI 10.3847/1538-3881/aae099

claims.title: Cosmic haystack framing
claims.detail: The paper described SETI search space as a high-dimensional haystack involving factors such as sky position, frequency, bandwidth, sensitivity, time, polarization, and modulation.

claims.title: Limited searched fraction
claims.detail: The authors estimated that only a tiny fraction of the relevant SETI search space had been searched.

claims.title: Non-detection interpretation
claims.detail: The paper argued that current non-detections should be interpreted in light of the small fraction of search space explored.

claims.title: Radio-focused scope
claims.detail: The analysis focuses on certain technosignature search dimensions and does not cover all possible forms of extraterrestrial technology or activity.

title: The G Infrared Search for Extraterrestrial Civilizations with Large Energy Supplies. III. The Reddest Extended Sources in WISE
source: Griffith et al. 2015; The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series 217:25; DOI 10.1088/0067-0049/217/2/25

claims.title: WISE infrared search
claims.detail: The study searched WISE data for galaxies with mid-infrared signatures that could be consistent with very large energy use.

claims.title: Galaxy-scale technosignature target
claims.detail: The search was motivated by possible waste-heat signatures of Kardashev Type III or galaxy-spanning civilizations.

claims.title: No obvious Type III detections
claims.detail: The study did not report clear detections of galaxy-spanning civilizations with very large infrared waste heat signatures.

claims.title: Candidate and astrophysical contamination
claims.detail: The paper discussed red infrared sources and the need to distinguish possible candidates from natural astrophysical sources such as dust-obscured galaxies.

claims.title: Search scope
claims.detail: The search constrains a particular class of high-energy, waste-heat-producing civilizations, not all possible technological civilizations.

title: The Sustainability Solution to the Fermi Paradox
source: Haqq-Misra and Baum 2009; Journal of the British Interplanetary Society 62:47-51; arXiv:0906.0568

claims.title: Sustainability explanation
claims.detail: The paper proposed that long-lived civilizations may adopt sustainable development patterns rather than rapid exponential expansion.

claims.title: Expansion assumption critique
claims.detail: The explanation challenges the assumption that advanced civilizations will inevitably expand rapidly across the Galaxy.

claims.title: Detectability implication
claims.detail: Civilizations following low-growth or sustainable trajectories may be less detectable than rapidly expanding high-energy civilizations.

claims.title: Civilization behavior dependence
claims.detail: The solution depends on assumptions about the long-term behavior, resource use, and growth strategies of technological civilizations.

title: The Fermi Paradox and the Aurora Effect: Exo-civilization Settlement, Expansion, and Steady States
source: Carroll-Nellenback et al. 2019; The Astronomical Journal 158:117; DOI 10.3847/1538-3881/ab31a3

claims.title: Settlement model
claims.detail: The paper modeled interstellar settlement dynamics rather than assuming instantaneous or uniform Galactic colonization.

claims.title: Stellar motion
claims.detail: The model incorporated the motion of stars through the Galaxy as a factor in settlement dynamics.

claims.title: Patchy settlement possibility
claims.detail: The paper found that settlement patterns can be non-uniform or patchy under some assumptions.

claims.title: Earth non-visitation compatibility
claims.detail: The authors argued that the absence of evidence for visitation of Earth can be compatible with settlement elsewhere in the Galaxy under some model conditions.

claims.title: Dependence on assumptions
claims.detail: The results depend on assumptions about spacecraft range, launch rates, settlement lifetimes, and whether settlements continue to generate further settlements.

title: The Great Filter - Are We Almost Past It?
source: Hanson 1998; online essay, George Mason University

claims.title: Great filter concept
claims.detail: Hanson described the Great Filter as one or more difficult steps between lifeless matter and large, visible, expansionist civilizations.

claims.title: Filter location question
claims.detail: The framework distinguishes between filters that may lie behind humanity and filters that may lie ahead.

claims.title: Observation of silence
claims.detail: The Great Filter framework uses the lack of observed large-scale extraterrestrial civilizations as a datum to be explained.

claims.title: Conditional interpretation
claims.detail: The meaning of extraterrestrial non-observation differs depending on which steps are rare or dangerous.
